note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Perform advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The roots of 30 m of double-sided butt welds in 20 mm carbon steel must be back gouged before the second side is welded. Which method is usually the most productive?
options: Cutting out the root with a cold chisel
Hand grinding the whole length with a flap disc
Air carbon arc gouging
Washing with a normal cutting nozzle

questions.stem: At the planned settings, one carbon electrode gouges about 300 mm of groove. How many electrodes should be drawn from stores for 12 m of gouging, with 10% spare?
Before a long air carbon arc gouging job, which check matters most for keeping the work going?
options: That the welding helmets in the team are all the same colour
That the job is done on the hottest day of the week
That every member has used the same torch before
That the power source, air and electrodes can last the job

questions.stem: A cracked area in a cast iron machine base must be removed before it is repaired. Which process is usually best?
options: Oxy-acetylene cutting
Air carbon arc gouging
Oxy-fuel gouging
Washing with a cutting tip

questions.stem: Why is plasma often preferred to air carbon arc for gouging stainless steel?
options: Plasma gouging needs no electric supply, so it is much safer
Plasma makes the stainless steel stronger than before
It leaves no carbon behind to harm corrosion resistance
Air carbon arc cannot make an arc on stainless steel

questions.stem: Why is oxy-fuel gouging not used on stainless steel or aluminium?
options: They do not burn away in an oxygen stream as steel does
Their surface is too shiny for the flame to heat it
They are too soft, so the nozzle sinks into the metal
Oxy-fuel gas is not allowed near non-magnetic metals

questions.stem: A trainee lets the stream of molten metal from gouging hit a damp concrete floor close by. Why is this a hazard?
options: The concrete will melt and flow back into the groove
The floor will become live and give an electric shock
The water will put the arc out and stop the gouging
Damp concrete can burst and throw out hot fragments

questions.stem: Why does air carbon arc gouging need stronger fume control than most arc welding?
options: Its fume is cooler, so it stays low near the welder's feet
It removes metal fast, so it makes a lot of fume quickly
The carbon electrode gives off a gas that is explosive
Its fume can only be cleared by opening the windows

questions.stem: When gouging overhead, which extra precaution matters most?
options: Gouging much faster, so that less molten metal falls down
Standing right under the joint so that it can be seen well
A fire-resistant cap, closed collar and standing aside
Turning the air off so that the molten metal does not spray

questions.stem: Why should the work return clamp be fixed close to the area being gouged?
options: So the current cannot pass through bearings, chains or hinges
So the clamp heats up and preheats the steel for the gouge
So the air hose and the cable can be tied neatly together
So the machine can run at a higher current than its rating

questions.stem: Why must the gouging current suit the carbon electrode diameter, as the maker's chart gives?
options: A higher current always gives a cleaner, smoother groove
Too high a current makes the groove narrower and deeper
Too low a current makes the copper coating last longer
Too low sticks and leaves carbon; too high burns it away fast

questions.stem: What happens if the air pressure is too low during air carbon arc gouging?
options: The electrode cools down too much and then the arc goes out
Molten metal is not blown clear and stays in the groove
The groove becomes very clean, smooth and shiny
The copper coating melts into the parent metal

questions.stem: A small portable compressor shows the right pressure until gouging starts, then the pressure falls and the groove fills with slag. What is the problem?
options: The air is too dry for the arc to burn properly
The pressure gauge is reading in the wrong units
The compressor cannot give enough air flow
The air pressure is too high and must be reduced

questions.stem: In which direction is a vertical joint usually gouged with air carbon arc?
options: Downwards, so the molten metal falls away from the groove
Upwards, so the molten metal runs back into the groove
Sideways only, as vertical gouging is not possible
Either way, since gravity has no effect on the molten metal

questions.stem: During gouging, the electrode touches the bottom of the groove (short-circuits) several times. What does this cause?
options: A cleaner, smoother groove that needs no grinding at all
A wider groove, which saves time when it is welded later
No effect, as long as the air is kept flowing
Hard carbon deposits in the groove that must be removed

questions.stem: A groove must be deeper than one gouging pass can safely make. What is the best method?
options: Hold the electrode still in one place until it is deep enough
Make two or more passes, each one cleaning out the last
Turn the current well above the maker's chart value
Push the electrode into the metal to dig it out

questions.stem: Which electrode shape is used to remove excess weld metal and leave a flat surface?
options: A round, pointed tungsten electrode
A round low-hydrogen stick electrode
A flat (rectangular) carbon electrode
A jointed round carbon electrode

questions.stem: A pipe end has been flame bevelled. What should be checked before it is fitted up?
options: Bevel angle, root face, squareness and clean metal
Only the colour of the cut face and the pipe length
Only that the pipe still rolls freely on the bench
The weight of the pipe and the depth of the drag lines

questions.stem: After back gouging the root of a double-sided butt weld, how do you confirm that sound metal has been reached?
options: Gouge to a set depth and assume the rest is sound
Weld over it, and test the finished weld later
Ask the welder whether the root felt good when welded
Inspect the groove, and use PT or MT if specified

questions.stem: What shape should a back-gouged groove have before it is welded?
options: A narrow, deep slot with sharp corners at the bottom
A smooth U, wide enough to reach the bottom
A shallow scratch along the line of the root
A V with a sharp point, as narrow as possible

questions.stem: While back gouging, you find a long line of slag deep in the first-side weld. What should be done?
options: Stop gouging and weld over it, as the cap will hide it
Leave it, because slag in the root is always allowed
Gouge until it is all removed, check and record it
Fill the groove with filler rod and melt it in

questions.stem: Why are small holes sometimes drilled just beyond each end of a crack before it is gouged out?
options: To stop the crack running further while it is removed
To let the air from the gouging torch escape
To mark where the welder should start the repair
To make the part lighter so that it distorts less

questions.stem: A procedure asks for preheat before gouging out a crack in a thick, high-strength steel beam. Why?
options: Preheat makes the carbon electrode last much longer
Preheat stops the cold air jet from cooling the arc down
Preheat makes the crack easier to see, by its bright colour
Fast cooling could harden and crack the groove

questions.stem: A temporary lifting lug must be removed from the wall of a finished steel tank. What is the right method?
options: Knock it off with a sledgehammer, then paint over the marks
Cut close to the wall, grind flush and check for cracks
Gouge deep into the tank wall to remove all the weld root
Leave it in place and tell the client it is a fixing point

questions.stem: When gouging out a defect for repair, why are the ends of the groove sloped gently rather than left square?
options: Sloped ends use fewer carbon electrodes
Square ends make the repair look untidy
So the welder can fuse the repair ends properly
So the inspector can see where the defect was

questions.stem: How is an oxy-fuel gouge started?
options: Heat a spot to red heat, then turn on the gouging oxygen
Turn on the gouging oxygen first, then light the flame
Strike an arc with the nozzle, then add the oxygen
Start on cold steel at full speed with the oxygen on

questions.stem: Why is the nozzle held at a low angle to the plate when oxy-fuel gouging?
options: To keep the flame away from the welder's gloves
To make the nozzle last longer before it is cleaned
To cut right through the plate as quickly as possible
So the oxygen stream scoops out a groove, not a kerf

questions.stem: Which statement about plasma gouging, compared with air carbon arc gouging, is correct?
options: It can only be used on mild steel, never on other metals
It leaves no carbon and works on non-ferrous metals
It needs a carbon electrode and a separate air hose
It needs no PPE because the arc is hidden in the torch

questions.stem: Why is a thick tee joint often prepared with a bevel on both sides of the web plate, rather than on one side only?
options: It lets the job be welded from one side only
It makes the joint easier to cut with one torch
It needs less weld metal and balances the shrinkage
It removes the need for any root face or gap

questions.stem: How can a cutting trolley cut a bevel and its root face in one pass?
options: Two torches: one upright for the root face, one angled
One torch held flat and parallel to the plate surface
One torch, with the trolley run twice as fast as normal
One torch, cutting upwards from underneath the plate

questions.stem: A WPS asks for a 30° ± 2.5° bevel. A flame-cut bevel measures 26°. What should be done?
options: Accept it, because 26° is close enough to the 30° asked for
Weld it as it is, with a much higher current
Scrap the plate and cut a new one at 35°
Grind it open, then check the angle and root face

questions.stem: A pipe end must be cut to fit onto the side of a larger pipe at 90°. What is used to mark the shape?
options: A straight line squared round the pipe
A template developed from the two diameters
A circle drawn with a compass on the end
A line drawn freehand by eye and then ground

questions.stem: A branch pipe is to be set on (sitting on top of) the main pipe. About what size is the hole cut in the main pipe?
options: Twice the outside diameter of the branch
The outside diameter of the main pipe
The inside diameter of the branch pipe
Half the inside diameter of the branch

questions.stem: Why is a large pipe usually cut by hand in sections, turning it between them?
options: So the torch can be held at the right angle in an easy position
So the pipe cools between sections and does not need preheat
So the drag lines on each section all point the same way
So that less cutting oxygen is used for the whole cut

questions.stem: Why is a template for hand-torch tracing made a set amount smaller or larger than the part?
options: Templates shrink when heated, so they must be oversize
The part always grows by 10% as it cools down
The inspector needs the template to be a different size
The torch runs against it, so the cut is offset from it

questions.stem: A flange with a centre hole is cut from plate. Why is the hole cut before the outside?
options: The hole is smaller, so it uses less oxygen
The part stays held, so the hole stays in place
The outside edge cools faster if it is cut last
The hole hides any marks left by the first cut

questions.stem: Why is a slot usually cut by first piercing or drilling a hole at each end?
options: To show the inspector where the slot will be
To let the steel cool down between the two cuts
To give clean round ends and a place to start
To save cutting oxygen by making less kerf

questions.stem: Which two things are mainly measured to grade a thermally cut face against a cut quality standard?
options: Squareness and surface roughness
The colour and the temperature of the face
The weight of the part and its hardness
The speed of the cut and the gas pressure

questions.stem: How should a batch of 50 profile-cut gussets be checked against the drawing?
options: Check only the first one, since all the rest must be the same
Weigh them all together and compare with the total
Check that they all fit into the same box for delivery
Check the first fully, then each one on a master template

questions.stem: Why should heavy mill scale and rust be cleaned off along the line of a cut on thick plate?
options: So the plate will not need any painting after the cut
They slow the start and spoil the quality of the cut
So the cut part weighs less on the delivery note
Because scale makes the oxygen pressure too high

questions.stem: Two trainees want to gouge side by side in one booth to finish faster. What should you decide?
options: Yes, as long as they both face the same way
Yes, if they take turns to hold the air hose
No: each needs space, screens and a safe direction
Yes, but only if they both wear ear protection

questions.stem: What should be recorded on a weld repair record after a defect has been gouged out and re-welded?
options: Location, defect, size removed, inspection result and names
Only the date and the number of electrodes that were used
Only the name of the welder who made the first weld
Nothing, as a repaired weld is the same as a new one

questions.stem: Before gouging, you find that the insulation on the gouging torch is cracked near the jaws. What should you do?
options: Wrap it with electrical tape and carry on carefully
Use it, but wear two pairs of gloves for the job
Use it for short gouges only, then report it later
Take it out of use, tag it and have it repaired

questions.stem: Why is air carbon arc gouging not usually used to cut plate to size?
options: It cannot pass through any plate thicker than 3 mm
It gives a wide, rough cut and uses a lot of electrode
It only works on the edges of a plate, never in the middle
It leaves the cut edge too hard to be bent later on

questions.stem: A gouging job will be done on a site with no compressed air supply. What must the plan include?
options: Bottled oxygen to use in place of the compressed air
A plan to gouge with no air, at a much lower current
A portable compressor with enough flow, sited clear of fumes
A hand pump for each member to pump up the air

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What name is given to a pipe end that is cut to fit onto the curved side of another pipe?
What is the full name of the process that uses an arc from a copper-coated carbon electrode and a jet of compressed air to remove metal?
What do we call removing the root of a weld from the back so that the second side can be welded onto sound metal?
Which test uses a red dye and a white developer to show cracks at the surface of a gouged groove?
Which letter names a groove with one curved side and one straight side, cut on one plate of a tee or corner joint?
A gouging pass runs at 750 mm per minute. How many minutes of arc time are needed to gouge 9 m?
What name is given to carbon electrodes with a socket at one end and a peg at the other, so a new one can be fitted onto the stub?
What is the name for the total angle between the two bevelled faces of a butt joint?
What part is fitted to a plasma torch in place of the normal cutting tip when the torch is used for gouging?
What is the name of the device that carries a cutting torch along a track at a steady speed for straight and bevel cuts?
What do we call the length of carbon electrode sticking out beyond the jaws of the gouging torch?
Under its copper coating, what material is a gouging electrode mainly made of?
What is the name of the flexible band wrapped round a pipe so that a true square line can be marked on it?
What word names removing a thin surface layer of metal to take out defects such as seams or cracks?
What name is given to a butt joint preparation with a bevel on both sides of each plate, so that it looks like two Vs point to point?

essays.stem: Your team must back gouge and re-weld 20 m of double-sided butt welds in 25 mm steel plate in the workshop. Explain how you would plan the job: the method, equipment, safety, order of work, inspection and records.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose air carbon arc gouging, as it is fast on this length and thickness, and read the WPS for any preheat and for how the gouged root must be checked. I would check that the power source can run the electrode size at the maker's current for long periods, that the compressor gives enough air flow, and that there are enough electrodes, grinding discs and spares. I would plan a screened gouging area with fume extraction, a clear zone in the direction of the molten metal, nothing that can burn nearby, and an extinguisher. Each person would need full PPE, including hearing protection and a fire-resistant cap. I would plan the order of work so that gouging and welding are done in sections in a balanced order to limit distortion. Each gouged section would be ground clean and inspected, by PT or MT if specified, before welding. I would keep a record of each section: who gouged and welded it, what was found and the inspection results.
markingPoints: Chooses a suitable process and reads the WPS for preheat and inspection needs
Checks power source, air flow, electrodes and spares can last the job
Plans a safe area: screens, fume extraction, clear zone, fire precautions, full PPE including hearing protection
Plans a balanced order of work in sections to limit distortion
Grinds and inspects each groove before welding, and records each section

essays.stem: A crack about 80 mm long has been found at the toe of a fillet weld on a structural steel bracket. Explain how you would remove it by gouging and prepare the area for a repair weld.
essays.modelAnswer: First I report the crack and get an approved repair method, because the bracket is structural. I clean the area and find the true length of the crack, using dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing, since cracks are often longer than they look, and I mark both ends. If the procedure asks for it, I drill a small hole just beyond each end to stop the crack running, and I preheat the area to the temperature in the procedure. Then I gouge along the crack with air carbon arc, in shallow passes, until it has all gone. The groove should be a smooth U-shape with gently sloped ends so the welder can fuse it properly. I grind the groove to remove the carbon-rich layer and any hard skin, then check it again with dye penetrant or MT to prove that no crack is left. I measure the groove, record its location, length and depth, and pass it for welding. After the repair it is inspected again.
markingPoints: Reports it and works to an approved repair method
Finds the full extent with PT or MT and marks the ends; stop holes and preheat if the procedure asks
Gouges in shallow passes until the crack is fully removed
Smooth U-groove with sloped ends; ground clean
Re-checks with PT or MT, records the excavation and inspects after the repair

essays.stem: A trainee's air carbon arc gouges show (1) shiny black carbon deposits in the groove, (2) molten metal and slag left in the groove, and (3) an uneven, wavy groove. Explain the likely cause of each fault and how you would correct it.
essays.modelAnswer: Carbon deposits are usually caused by the electrode touching the work, often because the arc is too short or the trainee pushes the electrode in, or by a current too low for the electrode size. I would show the trainee how to keep a short, steady arc without touching, and set the current to the maker's chart. The deposits must be ground out before welding, because carbon can cause cracking. Molten metal and slag left in the groove usually mean the air is not doing its job: the air valve is not fully open, the pressure or flow is too low, or the air jets are not on the work side of the electrode. I would check the compressor, the hose and the torch set-up, and the angle of the electrode. An uneven, wavy groove usually comes from an unsteady hand, an uneven travel speed or a changing electrode angle. I would have the trainee practise on scrap with a steady body position, supporting the torch arm, and moving at an even speed while watching the groove.
markingPoints: Carbon deposits: electrode touching or current too low; keep a short arc, set the correct current, grind deposits out
Slag and metal left: low air pressure or flow, valve not fully open, or air jets on the wrong side
Corrects the air supply and torch set-up
Wavy groove: unsteady hand, uneven speed or changing angle
Gives practical coaching: practise on scrap with a steady position and even speed

essays.stem: Explain how you would mark out and cut a set-on branch connection at 90°: the saddle on the end of the branch pipe and the hole in the main pipe. Include how you would check the fit.
essays.modelAnswer: For the saddle, I develop a template from the outside diameter of the main pipe and the size of the branch, either by drawing the development or using a template the Centre has checked. I cut the template from thin card or sheet, wrap it round the branch with its base line square to the pipe axis, using a wrap-around to mark a true square line first, and mark the shape with soapstone or a scriber. For the hole, I mark the centre lines on the main pipe and mark a hole about the size of the bore of the branch, since the branch sits on top. I centre punch the marks so they are not lost. I cut the hole first by piercing in the waste, then follow the line with the torch pointing towards the centre of the main pipe. I cut the saddle with the torch angled to suit the joint and the bevel needed. I clean off slag, grind to the line, and check the fit: the gap should be even all round, the branch square in both directions, and the bevel and root face as the WPS says.
markingPoints: Develops or uses a checked template from the two pipe sizes
Marks the saddle from a true square base line using a wrap-around
Marks the hole about the size of the branch bore for a set-on branch; centre punches the marks
Cuts the hole (pierce in the waste) and the saddle with the correct torch angles
Cleans up and checks the fit: even gap, square both ways, bevel and root face to the WPS

essays.stem: You are leading gouging work in a busy shared workshop with other trades working nearby. Explain how you would plan the work area and protect your team and everyone else.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first agree the time and place with the other trades and the supervisor, and get a hot work permit if the workshop uses them. I would choose a spot where the molten metal can be thrown into a clear zone, away from walkways, gas cylinders, hoses, cables and anything that can burn, and away from damp concrete. I would surround the area with fire-resistant screens to stop arc light and sparks reaching others, and put up warning signs. Fume extraction would be set up at the work, as gouging makes a lot of fume, with respirators where the extraction is not enough. Noise is very high, so my team wears ear plugs and muffs, and nearby workers are warned or given protection. The return clamp goes close to the work, and cables and air hoses are routed so nobody trips. A charged extinguisher is kept at hand and someone watches for fires during and after the work. At the end, stubs are put in a metal container and the area is checked before we leave.
markingPoints: Agrees time and place with others and the supervisor; hot work permit if used
Chooses a safe area with a clear zone for the molten metal, away from flammables, cylinders and damp concrete
Screens and signs to protect others from arc light and sparks
Fume extraction, hearing protection for the team and warning for others
Fire precautions during and after; cables and hoses routed safely; area checked at the end

essays.stem: Your team must cut 50 identical gussets from 12 mm plate with a hand torch. Explain how you would make and use a template, and how you would check the batch.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make the template from steel sheet or flat bar, thick enough to guide the torch without warping. Because the torch runs against the template, the cut is offset from its edge by the distance from the side of the nozzle or guide to the centre of the cut, minus half the kerf. I would work out this offset from a trial cut and make the template that much smaller (for an outside shape) than the gusset, then check it carefully against the drawing and mark it with the job number. I would lay out the gussets on the plate to use it well, leaving room for the kerf. Each gusset is cut with the template clamped firmly, keeping the nozzle at a steady height and angle, and with holes or slots cut before the outside. The first gusset is checked fully against the drawing before the rest are cut. After that, each gusset is checked on a master gusset or template, and every tenth one is measured fully. Any that are out of tolerance are marked and set aside.
markingPoints: Makes a rigid template and allows for the offset between the template edge and the cut (from a trial cut)
Checks the template against the drawing and marks it
Lays out the parts to save plate, allowing for the kerf
Cuts with the template clamped, steady nozzle height and inner features first
Checks the first part fully, then each part on a master, with regular full checks; rejects set aside

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose and cut the edge preparation for butt and tee joints in thick steel plate (for example 25 mm), and how you would check it before fit-up.
essays.modelAnswer: The WPS sets the preparation, but the reasons matter. A single-V is simple to cut, but on thick plate it needs a lot of weld metal and pulls the plate out of line as it shrinks. A double-V (or, on a tee, a bevel on both sides of the web) needs about half the weld metal and the shrinkage on the two sides balances, but the joint must be reachable from both sides and the root is usually back gouged. A U or J preparation needs even less weld metal on very thick plate but is harder to make. I would cut the bevels with a cutting trolley on a track, with the nozzle at the bevel angle and a second, upright torch for the root face if available, after a trial cut to set the speed. I would clean off slag and grind the faces bright. Then I check the bevel angle with a bevel gauge, the root face with a rule or gauge, and the edge for straightness and notches, and record that it meets the WPS before fit-up.
markingPoints: Follows the WPS and explains single-V versus double-V or double bevel (weld metal, balanced shrinkage, access, back gouging)
Mentions U or J preparations for very thick plate
Cuts with a trolley at the set angle, with a trial cut and a root face
Cleans and grinds the faces
Checks bevel angle, root face, straightness and notches and records it

essays.stem: Describe how you would remove a temporary lifting lug and its welds from the wall of a finished steel tank without harming the tank, and how you would check the area afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the drawing or procedure for how lugs are to be removed, and whether preheat is needed for the tank steel and thickness. I make sure the lug is not carrying any load and that the tank is clean, gas-free and safe for hot work, with a permit if needed. I cut or gouge the lug off a few millimetres away from the tank wall, never into it, so that the tank plate is not nicked. I then grind the remaining weld metal down flush with the wall, taking care not to grind below the surface of the plate. I check the area by eye and with a straight edge for any dip or nick, and measure the plate thickness if there is any doubt. Because cracks can form where temporary welds were, I check the area with dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing as the specification says. Any defect found is repaired by an approved method. I record the removal and the inspection results, and the area is then primed and painted to match the rest.
markingPoints: Checks the procedure (method, preheat) and that the lug is unloaded and the tank safe for hot work
Cuts or gouges a few millimetres clear of the wall, never into it
Grinds flush without going below the plate surface
Checks for nicks and thinning, and for cracks with PT or MT
Repairs any defect by an approved method, records it and restores the coating

essays.stem: Explain how the heat from gouging and thermal cutting can affect steel, and how you would prevent each problem.
essays.modelAnswer: The steel next to a cut or gouge is heated very quickly and then cooled quickly by the surrounding metal. On high-carbon or high-strength steels this can make the surface hard and brittle, and small cracks can form. This is prevented by preheating as the procedure says, and by grinding off the hard layer before welding or bending. Air carbon arc gouging can leave a thin carbon-rich layer and carbon deposits in the groove, which can make the weld crack, and on stainless steel can lower its resistance to rust. This is prevented by keeping a steady arc that does not touch the work, grinding the groove clean before welding, and using plasma or grinding on stainless steel. The uneven heating also causes distortion: long thin strips bow, and plates heated on one side bend. This is controlled by clamping, cutting both sides of a strip together, leaving tabs, and gouging and welding in a balanced order. Overheating for a long time can also coarsen the grain, so heat should be kept local.
markingPoints: Fast heating and cooling can harden and crack the edge on high-carbon or high-strength steel; prevented by preheat and grinding
Carbon pick-up from air carbon arc can cause cracking, and harm stainless steel; prevented by good technique, grinding, or plasma or grinding on stainless
Uneven heating causes distortion
Distortion controlled by clamping, balanced cutting or gouging, tabs and sequence
Keeps heat local to avoid grain growth

essays.stem: Two trainees in your team are to do their first air carbon arc gouging. Describe how you would brief, supervise and assess them.
essays.modelAnswer: Before they start, I would explain the process, the hazards and the controls: noise, fume, molten metal, fire, arc light, electric shock and burns, and the PPE needed, including hearing protection and a fire-resistant cap. I would show them the set-up: the polarity, the current for the electrode size from the maker's chart, the air supply, the air jets on the work side of the electrode, the stick-out, and where the molten metal will go. I would then demonstrate a straight groove on scrap plate while they watch from a safe place with suitable eye protection. Each trainee would then set up and gouge on scrap while I stand beside them, ready to stop the work. I would check their position, angle, speed and arc length, and give short, clear feedback after each run. I would check each groove for depth, evenness and carbon deposits, and only let them gouge on a job once their grooves are consistently good. I would record their progress and sign off what they have shown they can do.
markingPoints: Briefs the hazards, controls and PPE, including hearing protection
Shows the correct set-up (polarity, current from chart, air, jets, stick-out, molten metal direction)
Demonstrates on scrap, then supervises closely and is ready to stop the work
Checks technique and the grooves, giving clear feedback
Allows job work only when competent; records progress

practical1.title: Back gouge a welded butt joint and excavate a marked defect, with a method plan and a repair record
practical1.brief: With the instructor present, the group plans and carries out air carbon arc gouging on two welded test pieces prepared by the assessor: (A) a butt joint in 12–20 mm carbon steel plate, about 600 mm long, welded from one side only; and (B) a plate with a weld in which the assessor has marked a length of 'defect' to be removed. Part 1, planning (about 45 minutes): write a short method plan giving the electrode size and the current from the maker's chart, the polarity, the air supply, the gouging order, the safe direction for the molten metal, the PPE and fire precautions, and how each groove will be checked. Part 2, gouging: set up the station and check it with the assessor; then each member back gouges at least 150 mm of joint A to sound metal, in one or more passes, keeping a smooth U-shaped groove, and the group removes the marked defect in piece B with gently sloped ends. Part 3, checking: grind the grooves clean, measure their depth and width at set points, check them by eye and by dye penetrant if the Centre has it, and fill in a repair record for each groove. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Test piece A: butt joint in 12–20 mm carbon steel, about 600 mm long, welded from one side only
Test piece B: plate with a weld and a marked defect length, from the assessor
Welding power source suitable for gouging, set to the polarity the electrode maker gives
Air carbon arc gouging torch and copper-coated carbon electrodes (size as the assessor chooses)
Compressed air supply with enough flow for the electrode size
Angle grinder with grinding discs; rule, depth gauge or weld gauge
Dye penetrant kit (if available); method plan and repair record forms
Fire-resistant screens, fume extraction, fire extinguisher and a metal container for stubs
photos: The gouging station set up, with screens, extraction and the clear zone
Each member gouging, in full PPE, from a safe angle
The back-gouged groove on piece A before grinding
The excavated defect on piece B, showing the sloped ends
A depth measurement on a ground groove
The completed repair records and the cleaned-up area
checklist: Helped write a method plan that matches the maker's chart and the Centre's rules
Wore full PPE, including hearing protection and a fire-resistant cap
Set up and checked the torch, air jets, current and return clamp correctly
Gouged a steady, even U-shaped groove without carbon deposits
Reached sound metal, or fully removed the marked defect, with sloped ends
Measured and inspected the groove and recorded the results accurately
Left the area safe: power off, air off, stubs in a metal container, fire check done
safety: Gouge only with the instructor present, behind fire-resistant screens, with the molten metal aimed into a clear zone
Wear full PPE: helmet with a suitable shade, ear plugs and muffs, fire-resistant cap and jacket, leather gloves and boots
Use fume extraction at the work; keep your head out of the fume
Remove anything that can burn, keep gas cylinders and hoses well away, and keep the molten stream off damp concrete
Keep an extinguisher at hand and check the area for smouldering material after the work

practical2.title: Develop and cut a pipe branch saddle and its hole, and flame bevel a pipe end, with an inspection record
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a length of main pipe and of branch pipe (for example 114 mm and 60 mm outside diameter, or the Centre's stock) and a sketch of a set-on branch at 90°. As a group: (1) develop the saddle template from the two pipe sizes, cut it from card or thin sheet and check it against the main pipe; (2) using a wrap-around, mark a square base line on the branch, then mark the saddle from the template; (3) mark the centre lines and the hole on the main pipe, about the size of the branch bore, and centre punch the marks; (4) with an oxy-fuel cutting set, cut the hole by piercing in the waste, cut the saddle on the branch, and flame bevel the end of a second piece of pipe to the angle and root face the assessor gives; (5) clean up and grind to the lines; (6) fit the branch to the main pipe without welding and check the gap all round, the squareness in both directions, and the bevel angle and root face, and record the results on an inspection record. Share the work so every member marks or cuts at least one feature while the assessor watches, and checks another member's work. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Main pipe and branch pipe lengths (for example 114 mm and 60 mm outside diameter), plus a short piece for bevelling
Oxy-fuel cutting set with flashback arrestors and hose check valves, cylinders secured upright
Card or thin sheet, scissors or snips, and drawing instruments for the template
Wrap-around, soapstone or scriber, centre punch and hammer, tape and rule
Angle grinder with grinding discs, bevel gauge, square and feeler gauges
photos: The developed saddle template checked against the main pipe
The saddle and the hole marked out and centre punched
A member cutting, in full PPE, with the work secured
The cut saddle and the cut hole after cleaning
The bevelled pipe end with the bevel gauge in place
The branch fitted to the main pipe, showing the gap all round
checklist: Developed or checked the template accurately from the two pipe sizes
Marked a true square base line with the wrap-around and marked out accurately
Checked the cutting set (hoses, arrestors, connections) and lit and shut it down as the maker and the Centre's rules say
Cut to the line with the torch at the right angle for each feature
Bevel angle and root face within the tolerance the assessor set
Fit-up: even gap and branch square in both directions
Recorded results accurately and checked another member's work
safety: Check the cutting set before use, with flashback arrestors fitted; keep cylinders chained upright and hoses out of the path of sparks and slag
Wear cutting goggles or a face shield with a suitable shade, leather gloves, a fire-resistant jacket and safety boots
Secure the pipe so it cannot roll, and cut with the slag directed away from people, hoses and anything that can burn
Keep an extinguisher at hand; treat all cut pipe as hot and mark it
Wear safety glasses and a face shield when grinding, and check the disc is right for the grinder
